items.title: FCA Handbook, SYSC 15A: Operational resilience
items.quote: in the event of a severe but plausible disruption to its operations
items.why: The binding rule for firms in scope: identify important business services, set an impact tolerance for each, map the people, processes and technology behind them, test against severe but plausible scenarios and run a lessons learned exercise. Applies to the firms listed in SYSC 15A.1, not to businesses generally.

items.title: Operational resilience
items.locator: Opening section and 'Operational resilience requirements for firms'; last updated 15 September 2026
items.quote: Firms in scope of our operational resilience rules had until 31 March 2025
items.why: Source of the deadline in the brief. Defines operational resilience as the ability to prevent, adapt and respond to, and recover and learn from operational disruption, and explains impact tolerances as the maximum tolerable disruption.

items.title: CrowdStrike outage: lessons for operational resilience
items.locator: Sections 'Our general observations following the outage' and 'Observations on ensuring the resilience of infrastructure'
items.quote: Firms reflected on the need to identify single points of failure within their infrastructure and technology stack
items.why: The UK regulator's review of the 19 July 2024 outage. Firms that had mapped their important services and tested severe scenarios recovered faster. It reports that third-party issues were the leading cause of operational incidents reported between 2022 and 2023. Financial sector only; no AI system was involved.

items.title: Critical third parties: strengthening UK financial services
items.locator: Sections 'What the regime means' and 'Designated Critical Third Parties'
items.quote: Firms remain responsible for managing their own third-party risks in line with our existing operational resilience and outsourcing requirements.
items.why: Concentration risk in law. Designation regulations came into force on 13 July 2026 for four providers (Amazon Web Services EMEA SARL, Google Cloud EMEA Limited, Microsoft Ireland Operations Limited, Oracle Corporation UK Limited). Oversight covers their systemic services to the financial sector only and does not move responsibility away from the firm.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 32: Security of processing
items.quote: the ability to restore the availability and access to personal data in a timely manner in the event of a physical or technical incident
items.why: The one general legal duty that touches recovery: where personal data is processed, security measures include, as appropriate, resilience of systems, timely restoration and regular testing. It protects access to the data, not continuity of the service as such.

items.title: Cyber Assessment Framework, Principle B5: Resilient networks and systems
items.locator: Principle B5 description and guidance on resilience preparation; version 4.0, reviewed 6 August 2025
items.quote: consideration is also given to how operation of the essential function can continue in the event of technology failure or compromise
items.why: Source of the quotation. Names manual processes as contingency, asks for business continuity and disaster recovery plans that are tested, and for an understanding of the order of actions needed to restore service. Written for operators of essential functions.

items.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.quote: System Operators shall develop and tailor their disaster recovery plans to account for specific attacks aimed at AI systems.
items.why: The AI-specific recovery expectation. Provision 5.3.1 adds that operators should ensure that a known good state can be restored. Voluntary code; framed around attacks, not supplier outage or withdrawal of a model.

items.title: Cyber security breaches survey 2025/2026
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology and Home Office
items.quote: A similar proportion of businesses (33%), and a smaller proportion of charities (20%) had a business continuity plan that covered cyber security.
items.why: Source of the figure. Among small businesses the share fell from 53% to 44% in a year. The question is about continuity plans that cover cyber security; it does not ask about AI dependencies or whether the plan was tested.

items.title: Guidelines for secure AI system development
items.publisher: National Cyber Security Centre, with the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and partner agencies
items.locator: Section 2 'Secure development', 'Secure your supply chain' (PDF page 12); section 3 'Secure deployment', 'Develop incident management procedures' (PDF page 14)
items.quote: You are ready to failover to alternate solutions for mission-critical systems, if security criteria are not met.
items.why: International comparator: guidance issued jointly by the UK centre and agencies of other countries. Asks providers to have an alternative ready for mission-critical systems. Addressed mainly to providers of AI systems, so a deployer reads it as a question to ask suppliers.
